extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy; those studying Aristotelian ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies Aristotle's criteria for moral virtues (e.g., courage, self-mastery, liberality, magnificence), distinguishing mean states from excesses and defects and listing practical markers, motives, and counter-examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is a mean state in respect of objects inspiring boldness or fear; the Brave man chooses his line and withstands danger either because it is honourable or because not to do so is base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary object-matter is fear (especially pain); courage involves enduring painful things for the sake of honour. Courage is judged by proper relation to fear and confidence (neither excess nor deficiency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cowardice
rubrics_metrics.description: The coward exceeds in feeling fear (fears wrong objects, in wrong ways) and is deficient in confidence; he fears all things and is fainthearted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cowardice shows itself by taking flight when danger is truly fearful, and by being unduly affected by pain rather than honour; it is a vice (defect) opposite to the mean of courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rashness
rubrics_metrics.description: The rash man exceeds in confidence; he is precipitate, eager before danger, and when actually in danger falls away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rashness resembles courage superficially but lacks right deliberation and motive; rash persons affect boldness but do not withstand real fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feigning/Imitated Bravery
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who wish to appear brave and imitate the Brave man in points they can often exhibit a mixture of rashness and cowardice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appearances of bravery without right motive or habituation produce inconsistent behaviour (curious mixture of rashness and cowardice); imitation is not genuine virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage of Citizenship (honour-based courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage arising from regard for penalties, disgrace, or the dignities conferred by law and opinion—acting from shame and desire of honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplified in Homeric characters (Diomed, Hector); this form resembles true courage because it is motivated by honour, but is socially grounded rather than purely internal moral choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage under Compulsion (military compulsion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done under compulsion by commanders (threats, beatings, tactical placement) produce behaviour resembling courage but are motivated by fear of pain or penalty, not honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such behaviour is lower than true courage because the motive is avoidance of pain rather than choice for honour; commanders' compulsion produces obedience rather than moral bravery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage from Experience and Skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitual exposure, training, and technical skill (e.g., regular troops) produce a show of courage because such men are accustomed to seeing dangerous things and can inflict without suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates suggested 'courage is knowledge'—skill mitigates fear. But this is contingent: trained troops become cowards if danger exceeds their means; their apparent courage may be conditional on resources and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage from Animal Spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Impulsive boldness arising from 'animal spirit' or physical arousal (anger, blood boiling) can resemble courage but lacks moral choice and proper motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wild beasts or men goaded by pain or lust rush into danger; without rational deliberation and honour-motive this is not true courage, though animal spirit may cooperate with genuine courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger/Revenge-based Boldness
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold actions arising from anger or desire for revenge may produce good fighters but are not true courage because they act from present feeling, not from sense of honour or reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such persons act from immediate passion; while effective in conflict, they lack the morally directed motive that defines true courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanguine/Hopeful Boldness
rubrics_metrics.description: Boldness born of a settled conviction of superiority (or intoxication) — confidence from repeated victories — is not true courage because it collapses when expectations fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These people are confident due to calculation or habit rather than moral choice; when events disappoint them they will run away, unlike the truly brave who withstand fear for honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage under Sudden Fear vs. Anticipated Danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing fearlessness under sudden, unexpected danger is a greater proof of courage than preparedness for anticipated dangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreseen dangers allow calculation; steadfastness in sudden fear indicates a fixed habit of mind (true courage) rather than mere preparation or reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage under Ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions performed under ignorance (deceived about actual danger) give a show of courage and are nearer to the hopeful than to true courage, but are inferior because the agent lacks the right opinion of himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deceived fighters will flee when they realize the truth; ignorance-based bravery is conditional and not fully virtuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain as Central to Courage's Object
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage principally involves enduring painful things (death, wounds) rather than seeking pleasant ends; the brave endure pain because it is honourable to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more complete the virtue/happiness, the greater the pain at the thought of death, yet the truly brave choose honour despite that pain. Courage's end is not pleasure but choice amid painful circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery (temperance/reason-governed appetites)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mean state with respect to pleasures (chiefly bodily pleasures of Touch and Taste), in which the appetitive principle is obedient to Reason: desires occur at right times, in right ways, and in right proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes mental pleasures (honour, learning) from bodily; perfected self-mastery regulates bodily desires (eating, sex, sensual touch) so one neither indulges excessively nor is pained by their absence; the appetitive principle accords with reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of Self-Control (akrasia/unrestrained appetite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive taking of pleasure (especially bodily) — taking pleasure in wrong objects, excessively, or at wrong times — producing pain because desire accompanies loss and indulgence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More voluntary/culpable than cowardice because pleasure is an object of choice; resembles childish grasping; habitual indulgence increases desire and can expel reason entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect in Pleasure (insensibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lack of pleasure in things (taking less pleasure than one ought) is nearly imaginary and not a realistic vice among humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes animals and humans naturally distinguish flavors and pleasures; total insensibility is not typified in ordinary moral classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality (generosity regarding wealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mean state concerning the giving and receiving of wealth: the Liberal man gives to proper persons, in the right proportion, at right times, from a motive of honour, and with pleasure or without pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wealth here means things measured by money. Liberality values wealth instrumentally (to give), not for its own sake; receiving rightly (from proper sources) and not taking from improper ones is part of the virtue; the liberal may sometimes exceed in giving to help others but does so in proportion to means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prodigality
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess in giving and forbearing to receive (often combined with receiving from improper sources); spending on unrestrained gratification of passions—wasteful expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prodigality can be folly rather than moral baseness; prodigals do good to many but give in wrong manner (to flatterers or for pleasure) and thus are not truly liberal; may be correctable by habituation or change in circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stinginess (illiberality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defect in giving and excess in receiving (often seeking base gain); those who are over-careful about wealth, receiving from improper sources, or refusing to give where fitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stinginess has many modes (close-fisted, sparing, usurers, brothel-keepers); it is more common and harder to cure than prodigality. Stinginess is the contrary vice to liberality and often involves base-gaining and submission to disgrace for small advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtue like liberality but specifically concerned with great and costly expenditures: fitting, large-scale spending in good taste and proportion to the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive for scale — the magnificent man spends greatly, on works proportionate to expense, motivated by honour and pleasure, and with attention to beauty and fitness rather than minimal cost. Excesses are vulgar profusion, want of taste, or meanness.
